rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.stem: Study the given graph. It illustrates :
rows.figure: REQUIRED — the question IS the printed graph; the stem names no function at all. The curve rises from about \((-1, -\pi/2)\) through the origin to about \((1, \pi/2)\), with \((-1, 0)\) and \((1, 0)\) marked on the x-axis and \(\pi/2\), \(-\pi/2\) marked on the y-axis. NOTE this is a DIFFERENT graph from 65/7/1's Q1, which has horizontal asymptotes and keys arctan. Page idx 2.
rows.solution:
Read the picture rather than looking for a formula.
The curve exists only for \(-1 \le x \le 1\) — the points \((-1, 0)\) and \((1, 0)\) mark where the x-axis is crossed and nothing is drawn beyond them — it passes through the ORIGIN, it is increasing, and it runs from \(y = -\frac{\pi}{2}\) up to \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
That domain of \([-1, 1]\) rules out \(y = \tan^{-1} x\) at once (defined for every real \(x\), with horizontal asymptotes) and \(y = \sec^{-1} x\) as well (defined only for \(|x| \ge 1\), the exact opposite gap). It also rules out \(y = \cos^{-1} x\), which has the right domain but is DECREASING, runs from \(\pi\) down to \(0\), and never takes a negative value — it does not pass through the origin.
What is left matches perfectly: \(\sin^{-1} 0 = 0\), \(\sin^{-1}(1) = \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\sin^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{2}\), and the principal branch is increasing on \([-1, 1]\).
Hence the graph illustrates \(y = \sin^{-1} x\).

rows.stem: If \(f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sin^2 ax}{x^2}, & \text{if } x \ne 0 \\ 1, & \text{if } x = 0 \end{cases}\) is continuous at \(x = 0\), then the value of 'a' is :
rows.solution:
For f to be continuous at \(x = 0\), the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x \to 0\) must equal the value \(f(0) = 1\).
Rewrite the quotient so that the standard limit \(\lim_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1\) can be used:
\(\frac{\sin^2 ax}{x^2} = \left(\frac{\sin ax}{ax}\right)^2 \cdot a^2\).
As \(x \to 0\) we also have \(ax \to 0\) (for \(a \ne 0\)), so \(\frac{\sin ax}{ax} \to 1\) and
\(\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 1^2 \cdot a^2 = a^2\).
Continuity therefore requires \(a^2 = 1\), that is \(a = 1\) or \(a = -1\). Both values genuinely work, because only \(a^2\) enters the limit, so the answer is \(\pm 1\).
(Taking \(a = 0\) would make the limit \(0 \ne 1\), so that choice fails; and quoting only \(1\) or only \(-1\) discards a valid value.)

rows.stem: If R be a relation defined as \(a\,R\,b\) iff \(|a - b| > 0\), \(a,\ b \in \mathbb{R}\) then R is :
rows.solution:
Test the three properties on \(a\,R\,b \iff |a - b| > 0\). Since a modulus is never negative, \(|a - b| > 0\) says exactly that \(a \ne b\), so R is the relation 'is different from'.
REFLEXIVE: \(a\,R\,a\) would need \(|a - a| = 0 > 0\), which is false. So R is not reflexive — indeed it fails for EVERY a.
SYMMETRIC: \(|a - b| = |b - a|\), so \(|a - b| > 0\) holds precisely when \(|b - a| > 0\). Hence \(a\,R\,b \Rightarrow b\,R\,a\) and R is symmetric.
TRANSITIVE: take \(a = 1\), \(b = 2\), \(c = 1\). Then \(1\,R\,2\) and \(2\,R\,1\) both hold, but \(1\,R\,1\) does not, since \(|1 - 1| = 0\). So R is not transitive, and the combined description 'symmetric and transitive' fails too.
The only property R possesses is that it is symmetric.

The numerator \(a^x\) is, up to a constant, the derivative of \(a^x\), and the expression \(a^{2x} = (a^x)^2\) — that pairing is the signal to substitute.
Put \(t = a^x\). Then \(dt = a^x \log_e a\;dx\), so \(a^x dx = \frac{dt}{\log_e a}\), and \(1 - a^{2x} = 1 - t^2\). Hence
\(\int \frac{a^x}{\sqrt{1 - a^{2x}}}\,dx = \frac{1}{\log_e a}\int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}} = \frac{\sin^{-1} t}{\log_e a} + C\).
Restoring \(t = a^x\),
\(\int \frac{a^x}{\sqrt{1 - a^{2x}}}\,dx = \frac{\sin^{-1}(a^x)}{\log_e a} + C\),
which is the choice \(\frac{\sin^{-1}(a^x)}{\log_e a} + C\).
(Differentiating that expression returns the integrand, which is the quickest check. The form with \(\cos^{-1}\) differs from it by more than a constant only in sign, so it is an antiderivative of the NEGATIVE of the integrand; and dividing by \(a^x\) instead of by \(\log_e a\) does not differentiate back at all.)

The conditional probability gives the intersection: by definition \(P\!\left(\frac{A}{B}\right) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\), so
\(P(A \cap B) = P\!\left(\frac{A}{B}\right) \cdot P(B) = \frac{2}{5} \times \frac{3}{5} = \frac{6}{25}\).
By the addition theorem,
\(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{5} + \frac{3}{5} - \frac{6}{25} = \frac{5}{25} + \frac{15}{25} - \frac{6}{25} = \frac{14}{25}\).
By De Morgan's law \(A' \cap B' = \overline{A \cup B}\), so
\(P(A' \cap B') = 1 - P(A \cup B) = 1 - \frac{14}{25} = \frac{11}{25}\),
which is the choice \(\frac{11}{25}\).
(Note that A and B are NOT independent here: independence would need \(P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{5} \times \frac{3}{5} = \frac{3}{25}\), whereas it is \(\frac{6}{25}\). The value \(\frac{14}{25}\) is \(P(A \cup B)\) itself, not its complement.)

rows.stem: If \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -5 \\ -17 \end{bmatrix}\), then find matrix A.
rows.solution:
The matrix on the left is of order \(3 \times 2\) and the product is \(3 \times 1\), so A must be of order \(2 \times 1\). Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}\). Then
\(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3x - y \\ y \\ 2x - 3y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -5 \\ -17 \end{bmatrix}\).
Equating corresponding entries gives three equations:
\(3x - y = 2\), \(y = -5\), \(2x - 3y = -17\).
The second gives \(y = -5\) immediately, and substituting into the first,
\(3x + 5 = 2 \Rightarrow 3x = -3 \Rightarrow x = -1\).
Now TEST these values in the third equation, which has not yet been used:
\(2(-1) - 3(-5) = -2 + 15 = 13\), but the right-hand side is \(-17\).
The three equations are therefore inconsistent — no pair \((x, y)\) satisfies all of them — so there is no matrix A with the stated property. Hence the required matrix A does not exist.
[Note: the inconsistency is in the QUESTION's data, not in the working. The marking scheme reaches the same verdict by exactly this route, so 'A does not exist' is the expected answer; a student who finds \(x = -1\), \(y = -5\) from two of the equations and stops has not finished, because the third equation is what settles the matter.]

rows.subtopic: Derivatives of Implicit and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
rows.stem: Show that the derivative of \(\tan^{-1} (\sec x + \tan x)\), \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) with respect to x is equal to \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
rows.solution:
The neat route is to simplify the expression inside \(\tan^{-1}\) BEFORE differentiating; done directly the chain rule is very messy.
Write
\(\sec x + \tan x = \frac{1}{\cos x} + \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \frac{1 + \sin x}{\cos x}\).
Now express both parts through the same half-angle. Using \(\sin x = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\) and \(\cos x = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\),
\(\frac{1 + \sin x}{\cos x} = \frac{1 + \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)} = \frac{2\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{x}{2}\right)}{2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{x}{2}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{x}{2}\right)} = \cot\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{x}{2}\right)\),
using \(1 + \cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta\) and \(\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\) with \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{x}{2}\).
Since \(\cot\theta = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)\),
\(\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{x}{2}\right) = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{x}{2}\right) = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{x}{2}\right)\).
Therefore
\(\tan^{-1}(\sec x + \tan x) = \tan^{-1}\left(\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{x}{2}\right)\right) = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{x}{2}\),
and the cancellation is legitimate because for \(-\frac{\pi}{2} < x < \frac{\pi}{2}\) the angle \(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{x}{2}\) lies in \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), which sits inside the principal branch \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
Differentiating the resulting linear expression,
\(\frac{d}{dx}\left[\tan^{-1}(\sec x + \tan x)\right] = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{x}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\),
as required.

rows.stem: Find dimensions of a rectangle of perimeter 12 cm which will generate maximum volume when swept along a circular rotation keeping the shorter side fixed as the axis.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: the printed solution models the sweep by setting \(2\pi r = x\) — that is, it treats the longer side as the CIRCUMFERENCE of the cylinder, giving \(V = \pi\left(\frac{x}{2\pi}\right)^2 y\). Rotating a rectangle about one of its sides produces a cylinder whose RADIUS is the adjacent side, so the volume is \(\pi x^2 y\). The two expressions differ only by the constant factor \(4\pi^2\), and multiplying a function by a positive constant does not move its maximum, so the scheme still reaches the correct dimensions; only its volume figure would be wrong.]
Let the sides of the rectangle be \(x\) cm and \(y\) cm, with \(y\) the shorter side, which is held fixed as the axis. The perimeter condition gives
\(2(x + y) = 12 \Rightarrow x + y = 6 \Rightarrow y = 6 - x\).
Sweeping the rectangle a full turn about the side of length \(y\) generates a cylinder of height \(y\) whose radius is the other side, \(x\). So
\(V = \pi x^2 y = \pi x^2 (6 - x) = \pi\left(6x^2 - x^3\right)\), for \(0 < x < 6\).
Differentiating,
\(\frac{dV}{dx} = \pi\left(12x - 3x^2\right) = 3\pi x (4 - x)\).
Setting this to zero gives \(x = 0\) (rejected, it is not a rectangle) or \(x = 4\). For the second-derivative test,
\(\frac{d^2V}{dx^2} = \pi(12 - 6x)\), so at \(x = 4\) it is \(\pi(12 - 24) = -12\pi < 0\),
confirming a maximum.
Then \(y = 6 - 4 = 2\). Note this is consistent with the question: \(y = 2 < 4 = x\), so the side held fixed really is the shorter one.
Hence the rectangle measures \(4\) cm by \(2\) cm, with the \(2\) cm side as the axis (the resulting cylinder has volume \(\pi(4)^2(2) = 32\pi\) cubic cm).

The limits \(0\) and \(\pi\) with an \(x\) multiplying an otherwise symmetric integrand is the signal for the property \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx\).
Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{x \sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}\,dx\). Replacing \(x\) by \(\pi - x\), and using \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\) and \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\) (so \(\cos^2\) is unchanged),
\(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{(\pi - x)\sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}\,dx\).
Adding the two forms, the awkward factor \(x\) cancels:
\(2I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\pi \sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}\,dx \Rightarrow I = \frac{\pi}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos^2 x}\,dx\).
Now substitute \(t = \cos x\), so \(dt = -\sin x\,dx\); when \(x = 0\), \(t = 1\), and when \(x = \pi\), \(t = -1\). Hence
\(I = \frac{\pi}{2}\int_{1}^{-1} \frac{-dt}{1 + t^2} = \frac{\pi}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{dt}{1 + t^2} = \frac{\pi}{2}\left[\tan^{-1} t\right]_{-1}^{1}\).
Therefore
\(I = \frac{\pi}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi^2}{4}\).
So the value of the integral is \(\frac{\pi^2}{4}\), which is about \(2\cdot467\) — a positive number, as it must be, since the integrand is non-negative throughout \([0, \pi]\).

rows.stem: Solve the differential equation \((x^2 + y^2)\, dx + xy\, dy = 0\), \(y(1) = 1\).
rows.solution:
Every term of \((x^2 + y^2)\,dx + xy\,dy = 0\) has total degree \(2\) in x and y, so the equation is homogeneous and the substitution \(y = vx\) will separate it.
Writing it in derivative form,
\(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x^2 + y^2}{xy} = -\frac{1 + \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2}{\frac{y}{x}}\).
Put \(y = vx\), so that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}\). Then
\(v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = -\frac{1 + v^2}{v} \Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx} = -\frac{1 + v^2}{v} - v = -\frac{1 + 2v^2}{v}\).
Separating the variables,
\(\frac{v\,dv}{1 + 2v^2} = -\frac{dx}{x}\).
The left side is \(\frac{1}{4}\) of \(\frac{4v\,dv}{1 + 2v^2}\), whose numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator, so integrating gives
\(\frac{1}{4}\log\left(1 + 2v^2\right) = -\log|x| + \log C\).
Multiplying by \(4\) and combining the logarithms,
\(\log\left(1 + 2v^2\right) = \log\frac{C^4}{x^4} \Rightarrow 1 + 2v^2 = \frac{D}{x^4}\), where \(D = C^4\).
Restoring \(v = \frac{y}{x}\),
\(1 + \frac{2y^2}{x^2} = \frac{D}{x^4} \Rightarrow x^4 + 2x^2y^2 = D\), that is \(\left(x^2 + 2y^2\right)x^2 = D\).
Applying the initial condition \(y(1) = 1\): \(1 + 2 = D\), so \(D = 3\).
Hence the particular solution is
\(\left(x^2 + 2y^2\right)x^2 = 3\), i.e. \(x^4 + 2x^2y^2 = 3\).
Check by differentiating: \(4x^3 + 4xy^2 + 4x^2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\), and dividing by \(4x\) gives \(x^2 + y^2 + xy\frac{dy}{dx} = 0\), which is the original equation.
